problem_data.story:
THE HARPER PROTOCOL
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Rosewood, Nordavia, in a building that had once been luxury condominiums before the Economic Collapse. The wealthy families who'd owned them had fled to offshore havens. Now the units were subdivided and rented cheaply. Ariana Kim and her daughter lived comfortably enough, even during the harshest winters. During summer months, Ariana ran a small consulting business helping local entrepreneurs with design thinking workshops. She had built a modest client base. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the encrypted files she had brought with her to Nordavia. They didn't even know she wasn't a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Bianca was a girl of seven and they had just arrived. Then she only said she came from the southern provinces. She knew the names of southern Nordavian towns, and small facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim. Actually her previous residence was Lincoln, Calderon, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Yarnmouth Station in Xandria; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders, covering the small neural port behind her ear—evidence that a quantum processor lay embedded under her skin.

For Ariana Kim was one of the Jumpers.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this neural interface technology. Not the inventor—his name was Vincent Harper, and the effects produced by it were known as the Harper Protocol. In appearance the implant resembled a standard neural enhancement device. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be just that—a neural enhancement.

Yet it held the power to move consciousness instantaneously from one body to any other prepared body across vast distances. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the specific neural pattern of the particular individual. The prepared bodies—clones grown in secret facilities—waited in cities across the world and beyond.

Several times in the past seven years Ariana had seen other Jumpers, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Harper and Santiago Spencer, who helped them all escape. And Doctor Walter Gutierrez. And my husband, Roman Frank, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that coffee shop in Lincoln, Calderon."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and rented the apartment next door.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While helping him move furniture, his identification badge fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly picked his lock and administered a lethal injection while he slept.

She disposed of the syringe in the city incinerator. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators across the world; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Bianca, was grown.

Together they would seek justice. Bianca did not have the implant—not yet. But she would. The Jumpers took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned, the small bandage would be behind her ear. Ariana would shield her until the incision healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek justice.

Later they would go to Yarnmouth Station in Xandria, where a life free from Regulators could be lived. The station orbited a distant moon, far from Earth's political economy and its oppressive systems.

It happened to Bianca one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Ariana was working in her home office on a design thinking presentation; Bianca supposedly was at the community center with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her mother, completely disoriented and wearing only a hospital gown. At sight of her mother, Bianca's face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Ariana was forced to hold her firmly to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her daughter's ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the community center, where her friends were still visible in the courtyard. Apparently they did not miss her. Ariana handed her a sweater. "Here, cover yourself. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Ariana stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well understand now."

"Understand what?"

"That your consciousness can now jump between bodies."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was at the center, and a woman came up to me. Her hair was all white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Bianca Hunter, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a car and there was another person in it, that looked like the first one only younger. We went to a clinic, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a medical table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some technical language I don't know."

Bianca ran her hand through her hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be home with you. And then I was here."

Bianca faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better sit down," Ariana said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful in terms of time management and career planning."

"But what happened? What is this port behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped moving. "I know now. They made me a Jumper."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Ariana called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side, about political philosophy and economic development. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator next door."

It was Ariana's turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw the syringe wrapper in your pocket the next morning. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Ariana held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So Bianca sat across the kitchen table from her, and Ariana told the whole history, beginning with Vincent Harper sitting in the laboratory in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, holding in his hand a neural implant he had designed for medical purposes. He had made it to help paralysis patients control prosthetic limbs. He was holding this device... and it was connected to a clone body in the next room for testing... and he was thinking about being young again—

And suddenly his consciousness was there, in the clone body. He could not believe it at first. He felt the young muscles and reflexes, and examined himself; there was no mistake.

On the flight back to his old body he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more implants. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it properly, and he kept the secret, giving implants to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it quantum-entangled consciousness transfer, which was very theoretical modeling.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for identity fraud. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that consciousness arrived in a clone body that looked nothing like the original.

The arrested man jumped to another body and disappeared, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead. This set off a campaign against Jumpers. One violent act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as trustworthy citizens.

Ariana told how Harper, knowing he had made too many implants and given them unwisely, left Earth for Yarnmouth Station in Xandria.

He went alone, not knowing if he could jump so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought—a place where political economy favored freedom over control.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in a warehouse in Rosewood—and their consciousnesses jumped in unison to clone bodies waiting at Yarnmouth Station, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at empty shells.

"You have asked many times," Ariana said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Harper and Spencer and Dr. Gutierrez. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Lincoln fifteen minutes before the group jumped. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator next door? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Bianca said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says 'Jumper' as if it is something dirty. They write it on bathroom walls."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them? It's basic consumer behavior and cultural sociology."

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Ariana watched Bianca leave the apartment, walking slowly along the street, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the community center, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would go to the park and sit by the fountain. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not jump far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within the city limits, because she still lacked the skills others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Ariana changed into lighter clothes and went for a walk to clear her mind.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, jumping to clone bodies in increasingly distant cities, until Bianca's confidence allowed her to reach any prepared body on Earth. Ariana knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a location sufficiently remote to ensure detection, Ariana would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly jump back to Rosewood. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only abandoned clone bodies. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Ariana as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Harper took his group to Xandria, that individuals had neural patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their scanners, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Ariana Kim had gone to Xandria with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Harper had selected only the most ethical Jumpers when he left Earth, leaving all those with criminal tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more profitable to stay. On Earth they could steal, extort, even murder—without fear of the law, since they could always jump to a new body.

Bianca changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Bianca," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Ariana would repeat all the things she remembered about Harper and Spencer and Gutierrez. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Spencer's partner, Zara Rivera, and try to describe the horror in Zara's young mind when the news went out that Roman Frank had been killed. She wanted Bianca to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after her. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of righteous anger.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Ariana wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Remember! Remember! You must never forget!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that Bianca would internalize it better if she avoided being too forceful.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Bianca was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Bianca referred to the "damn Regulators" now with contempt. They had been successful in contacting other Jumpers, and sometimes visited them at remote locations.

"When you have finished university," Ariana told her daughter, "we will go to Xandria together. That is our plan, and nothing will change it."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the development of the station. Harper is a neuroscientist, Spencer an engineer, Gutierrez a doctor. But Gutierrez is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Bianca. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Your knowledge of public health and organizational behavior will be invaluable."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Bianca would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she accessed the encrypted accounts she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Rosewood was abandoned. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Ariana furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Bianca's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of university students.

It was also convenient for jumping to clone bodies late at night after Regulator hunting.

Ariana was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Bianca facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were corrupt enforcers, tools of a decadent, authoritarian system, living off citizens' taxes.

She painted the room herself, in soft, calming colors. When it was finished she showed Bianca into the room with ceremony, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study groups students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," Bianca answered, "not here. No Jumpers will be at the university."

"Why not? Harper selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the implant is taken and adjusted to a new neural pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Jumpers will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Ariana said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable for your career planning."

Bianca shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

She said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being independent, at your age. Most young adults do."

"I'm not like most young adults, mother. The Jumpers saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Camila Singh?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how focused she was when she studied, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Camila—' just as if I was normal—'can I study with you for the exam?'"

Ariana turned to leave the room, but Bianca stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Jumper. You always will be a Jumper. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and left the room. Bianca stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been liberating for her. Her mother was crying just beyond the wall.

Bianca did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the implant was out of the question for them now, anyway—too risky with Regulators scanning constantly.

In the spring Ariana caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Bianca moved into the new bedroom. At first Ariana thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day Bianca disappeared.

Ariana was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Jumpers being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Jumper had raided the Regulator's office in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, killing three, and getting killed herself. Ariana immediately jumped to a clone body in Yarnmouth. She did not consider the risk. In Yarnmouth she obtained clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain woman had been a Lethonian Jumper, one of those left behind by Harper as ethically unsuitable. Her partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. She had gone completely insane and made the raid single-handedly. Ariana read the account of crimes committed by the woman and her partner, and determined to prevent Bianca from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she jumped back to her original body at home, Bianca was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that incident in Yarnmouth."

She shook her head.

Ariana stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a tablet. She was proud of her daughter's profile, determined and intelligent. Bianca tapped nervously on the desk.

"What did you do?" she asked.

Suddenly Bianca pushed the tablet away, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Lincoln, Calderon."

Ariana had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to access the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the men who killed Father." She said the word with difficulty. She was unaccustomed to thinking of him that way.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the tablet on her desk. Ariana, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches, evil sounds. "Marcus Webb" didn't sound evil; neither did "David Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Bianca to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for justice. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask how I broke in without triggering alarms. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Jumpers must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Jumpers? We hunt them because there is no prison that will hold a Jumper. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us. It's a matter of political philosophy and collective memory—we can coexist.'"

Ariana was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Ariana stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her daughter's arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Ariana gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. Bianca had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to herself. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the men were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over the world. In the hunting of Jumpers, some implants might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the implants gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to acquire them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the men on Bianca's list might have acquired an implant and were now Jumpers themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Marcus Webb had been killed by a Jumper. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Bianca's desk.

She took the tablet into Bianca's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. His name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Jumper is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Lincoln will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Bianca asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

Bianca removed her mother's hand from her arm. Her mother's grip was painfully tight. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me, doing their jobs. I can't hate them the way you do. It's not about economic history or aesthetic philosophy—it's just human nature."

Ariana's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped Bianca's face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Ariana breathing hard from the exertion, Bianca stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that her mother could hate so suddenly, viciously.

Ariana controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, taunting them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive through every city on Earth with those new scanners, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Bianca sat down suddenly. "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no one can live this way."

She did not answer. Finally Bianca said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's arrival. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was there. Bianca saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely white. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to be. She was wearing simple clothes... but carried herself with quiet authority.

Then Ariana saw her.

"Zara!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said to Bianca, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was so nervous."

Bianca said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were ethical Jumpers and criminals. One of those not selected by Harper to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two people there in Lincoln. The Regulators thought Roman Frank—I mean, your father—did it. Frank was the greatest man among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the implants. Even now, no one fully understands how intention and purpose tie in with the Harper Protocol; but we do know that hatred and greed as motivating forces can greatly minimize the implants' power. That is why the criminals with implants have never reached Xandria."

Heavy footsteps sounded in the hallway outside.

"We'd better hurry," Ariana said.

Zara held out her hands. They took them, to increase the synchronization of the implants. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Ariana flicked one thought of hatred at them. Zara's hands gripped tightly. The pounding intensified.

Ariana felt the familiar pull of the jump beginning—the strange sensation of consciousness lifting away from flesh. She concentrated on Xandria, on the waiting clone bodies, on freedom. But something was wrong. The pull felt weak, distant. She gripped harder. The door splintered.

The sensation faded. Ariana slowly opened her eyes.

She was still in the room. Zara and her daughter were gone. Her outstretched hands touched nothing but empty air.

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. They raised their weapons.

She stood frozen, her mind racing through fragments of memory—something Zara had said about the Protocol, something about hatred and intention. There had been so much she wanted to tell Bianca. About Xandria. About the plan.

She reached toward Bianca's desk.

The Regulators' weapons fired.
